newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: ATHLETICS-PEREZ WORKS HARD TO KEEP FEET ON THE GROUND.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-PEREZ WORKS HARD TO KEEP FEET ON THE GROUND.

text.p: Ecuador's Olympic 20 km walk champion Jefferson Perez is working hard to keep his feet on the ground.
Not just because every major race suffers a plethora of disqualifications due to competitors failing to keep continous contact with the road but also because he has now won the sport's richest race.
The 23-year-old business administration student from the provincial city of Cuenca took the gold medal at the race walking World Cup on Saturday.
Perez also banked $20,000 on the first occasion that cash prizes have been on offer at the event, held this year in the Czech spa town of Podebrady.
He also won $15,000 for winning the Aztec Cup in Mexico City last month and the Ecuador government gave him $22,000 after he returned from Atlanta.
The World Cup was also Perez's fifth successive victory, a remarkable sequence in a sport where disqualifications are an occupational hazard.
In Podebrady, China's Mingjun Tan and Mexico's Bernardo Segura crossed the line in second and third place but were erased from the results after receiving red cards with the line in sight.
Since winning the world junior title in 1992, Perez has concentrated hard on honing his technique in order to avoid a similar fate.
He was elevated to celebrity status in Ecuador following his triumph in Atlanta, the first time any one from his country had won an Olympic gold medal, and his image appeared on a postage stamp.
Despite his successes, Perez still does not feel he has mastered his craft.
"I can't yet say that I am the world number one at this event because I have not yet reached the limits of athletics' excellence. I have a lot more potential."
"What would satisfy me? A world record certainly but I can go much, much faster."
The Ecuadorian government has invested heavily in its diminutive hero.
It has spent $100,000 on him in the last year, providing a nutritionist, physiologist, psychologist and extended the contract of his Colombian coach Enrique Pena, who was a 1980 Olympian.
A world championship gold medal this August in Athens, and maybe a world record, may just be the repayment with interest they are looking for.
